vignette:
Maria's Vigil

Maria sits in the waiting room with her hands folded in her lap, her posture rigid and alert. At fifty-four, she carries herself with the disciplined bearing of someone who has spent thirty years in the military. Her dark hair is pulled back tightly, and there's a watchfulness in her eyes that seems to scan the room even when she's trying to relax.

She enlisted at twenty-four, driven by a desire to prove herself in a field dominated by men. As a combat engineer, Maria specialized in explosive ordnance disposal and route clearance—work that demanded precision, courage, and an almost supernatural calm under pressure. For most of her career, she managed both. But that changed seven years ago during her fourth deployment to Afghanistan.

Maria's unit was clearing a route through Kandahar Province when the IED detonated. She was two hundred meters back when the blast erupted, throwing her squad leader and two younger soldiers into the air. The explosion itself wasn't what changed her—it was what came after. The screaming. The smell of burning flesh and dust. The way her hands moved on autopilot, applying tourniquets and calling for medevac, while her mind seemed to fracture into pieces that couldn't quite fit back together.

Two of the soldiers died before the helicopter arrived. Her squad leader, Sergeant Torres, survived but lost both legs. Maria had trained him herself five years earlier. She attended his funeral and watched his mother collapse into her husband's arms.

The years that followed were a slow unraveling. Maria completed her remaining service and retired with honors, but sleep became impossible. She would lie beside her husband, Roberto, listening to every creak in their house, certain something terrible was about to happen. When he reached for her in the dark, her body would jolt awake, adrenaline flooding through her as if mortars were falling outside their bedroom window in suburban San Antonio.

Work as a civilian contractor in infrastructure safety should have been manageable—it was still in her wheelhouse, still involved problem-solving and risk assessment. But Maria found herself unable to concentrate during meetings. Loud noises sent her heart racing. A car backfiring on the highway made her grip the steering wheel so hard her knuckles turned white. She'd pull over, hands shaking, unable to drive for hours.

The intrusive memories come without warning. She'll be standing in the grocery store, reaching for cilantro, and suddenly she's back in that moment—the earth heaving beneath her boots, the acrid smoke, the weight of Torres's arm around her neck as she dragged him toward cover. Her vision narrows. The fluorescent lights become unbearable. She abandons her cart and leaves.

Roberto has been patient, but Maria can see the worry etched into the lines around his eyes. He suggests things gently—therapy, medication, a support group for veterans. She resists. Part of her feels she doesn't deserve relief, that moving past this somehow dishonors the men who didn't make it out. Another part of her is terrified that if she stops staying vigilant, stops holding herself together through sheer force of will, everything will collapse.

Last month, Maria made an appointment. It took her three weeks to actually show up.

She sits in the waiting room now, palms sweating slightly, wondering if talking about it will make things worse or if she's finally ready to try.
